item.title: Dolpopa: Empty of Other
item.description:
An eight-chapter guided course on Dolpopa Sherab Gyaltsen (1292-1361), the master from Dolpo who taught emptiness of other: the Sakya education and the title Omniscient, the retreat where the zhentong view arose, the great stupa of Jonang and the first public teaching at the raising of the central poles, the Uttaratantra's charter verses, Dolpopa's own Seizing the Crucial Point of Every Utterly Perfect Discourse, the lineage before him (Yumo Mikyö Dorje, Tsen Kawoche), the Kālacakra described but not taught, the soul objection and Tāranātha's answers, the 1650 ban and the Amdo survival, the Rimé reopening, and the Third Karmapa's treatise with its later zhentong label flagged. An independent critical listening course: every doctrinal claim is labeled to its source, with Dolpopa's own words, the Indian texts he used, precursor and reception voices, and modern scholarship kept on separate shelves throughout. Realization and vision claims are reported as the tradition's own claims, never asserted as fact; there are no practice instructions anywhere in this course. Quotations are short and attributed; copyrights in the translations remain with their translators and publishers, and this release grants no rights in those texts. Narrated by Tara, an AI voice. item.title: Kant: The Law Within
item.description:
An eight-chapter guided course on Immanuel Kant: the clock of Königsberg and the young Kant of Swedenborg and Rousseau, the Copernican turn (synthetic a priori, space and time, appearances and things in themselves), the machinery of the categories and the walls of reason (causality, the antinomies, the God proofs, the three questions), the Groundwork's good will and categorical imperative, the fact of reason and the starry heavens, the third Critique on beauty and the sublime, the crooked timber of the political essays, and Kant's inheritance, with one explicitly labeled Buddhist comparison as a reading lantern. Narrated by Tara, an AI voice, with a special appearance by guest narrator Muse in five sections, volume matched. All primary works read from public-domain translations: the Groundwork and Prolegomena in full; the three Critiques, Religion, Dreams of a Spirit-Seer and the political essays in substantial selections; the Enlightenment essay in German with the course's own renderings, labeled. Anecdotes are labeled: the watch-setting walk and the Emile interruption are posthumous biographical tradition; the Swedenborg ghost stories are Kant's own hearsay report. Quoted material preserves the source translations' exact wording (for example, "requirest submission" in the Critique of Practical Reason passage); the surrounding narration modernizes archaic inflection. Original narration and commentary CC0 1.0 Universal; underlying translations are public domain (US, by publication date 1838-1903).

item.title: Khentrul Rinpoche: The Jonang Teachings
item.description:
Nine episodes, one course: love as enjoyment and compassion as fearlessness, death as daily practice, zhentong ('empty of other'), the Kalachakra and its Six Vajra Yogas at map level, Shambhala and the Golden Age, and how the Jonang school survived three centuries of being declared dead. An independent critical listening course on the public teachings of Shar Khentrul Jamphel Lodro Rinpoche: short attributed quotes, examined critically, including where the tradition's claims outrun verification. item.title: Plato: The Examined Life
item.description:
From Socrates's trial to the invisible ring, the divided soul, the cave and the philosopher-rulers: an introduction to Plato that takes the arguments seriously without excusing their political costs. Includes Diotima's account of love, the Phaedrus on writing, a source-honest translation note, and the myth of Er. History, dramatic presentation, myth and interpretation are kept distinct. Narrated by Tara, an AI voice. Provisional interpretation, not an authoritative translation, lineage transmission or practice authorization.
Full primary works read: the Apology and Crito in Benjamin Jowett's public-domain translation; the Republic, Symposium and Phaedrus appear as selected passages only, and the course says so - no whole-corpus claim. Socrates in the dialogues is a dramatic speaker, not a verbatim recording of the historical man. The oracle, the ring of Gyges, the cave, Diotima's account of Love's parentage, the Egyptian writing story and the myth of Er are attributed to their dramatic contexts, not treated as verified events. Moral and political criticism, present-day illustrations and the closing exercise are the course author's own interpretation and application. No long quotations; every argument is given in the course's own words. Original narration and commentary CC0 1.0 Universal.
Sources Plato, Apology, Jowett translation (Project Gutenberg): https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1656 Plato, Crito, Jowett translation (Project Gutenberg): https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1657 Plato, Republic, Jowett translation, selected passages (MIT Internet Classics): https://classics.mit.edu/Plato/republic.html Plato, Symposium, Jowett translation, selected passages (MIT): https://classics.mit.edu/Plato/symposium.html Plato, Phaedrus, Jowett translation, selected passages (MIT): https://classics.mit.edu/Plato/phaedrus.html Richard Kraut, "Plato", Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/plato/ "Plato's Ethics and Politics in The Republic", Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/plato-ethics-politics/ "Plato", Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: https://iep.utm.edu/plato/

item.title: Aryadeva: Crash Course
item.description:
Aryadeva, traditionally called Madhyamaka's second founder: the Sri Lankan prince of the biographies, the gift of an eye, the one-eyed verse that challenges three-eyed Shiva, and a debate legend ending in conversion. Alongside these stories stands the Four Hundred Verses and its reception in India, Tibet and China. A brief, honest course on a half-legendary giant, with every layer labeled. Narrated by Tara, an AI voice. Provisional interpretation, not an authoritative translation, lineage transmission or practice authorization.
The life stories are labeled legend throughout and drawn from Taranatha's seventeenth-century History of Buddhism in India, read in Anton Schiefner's public-domain 1869 German translation, and from W. P. Wassiljew's public-domain 1860 account of the Chinese tradition; every used detail was verified against those texts. The one-eyed verse belongs to Bu-ston's parallel account and is paraphrased, not quoted, and labeled second-hand in the episode. The contents of the Four Hundred Verses are described from the Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism entry, labeled second-hand; no verses are quoted. The four-suns comparison follows E. B. Cowell's public-domain 1894 report of Xuanzang. Aryadeva's dating is stated in the episode as inference from his teacher. Original narration and commentary CC0 1.0 Universal.

item.title: Spinoza: God or Nature
item.description:
